question: Workload Classification: Give two real-world examples of an I/O-bound task and two examples of a CPU-bound task in backend engineering.

options.text: - I/O-Bound: Fetching data from an HTTP REST API; writing large files to an SSD. - CPU-Bound: Image compression / resizing; cryptographic hashing / mathematical matrix operations.
- I/O-Bound: Compressing a video file; computing SHA-256 hashes in a loop. - CPU-Bound: Waiting on a database query over the network; reading a config file from disk.
- I/O-Bound: Any task that uses the print() function. - CPU-Bound: Any task that uses a for loop, regardless of what happens inside the loop body.
- I/O-Bound: Tasks that finish in under one second. - CPU-Bound: Tasks that take longer than one second to complete, regardless of whether they wait on external resources.

question: The GIL: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython, and why does it prevent multiple threads from executing pure CPU calculations simultaneously?

options.text: The GIL is a mutex that prevents multiple native OS threads from executing CPython bytecode at the same time, protecting Python's internal memory management (reference counts) from corruption.
The GIL is a per-object lock that CPython acquires only when two threads try to mutate the exact same variable at the same time; unrelated variables can still be modified fully in parallel.
The GIL is a feature of the operating system's thread scheduler, not CPython itself; it exists because Windows and Linux both cap Python processes at one core by default.
The GIL only restricts I/O operations like file reads and network calls to a single thread at a time; pure CPU-bound Python bytecode can already run fully in parallel across threads.

explanation: Specification answer: The GIL is a mutex that prevents multiple native OS threads from executing CPython bytecode at the same time, protecting Python's internal memory management (reference counts) from corruption.

question: I/O Concurrency: If the GIL exists, why does ThreadPoolExecutor still speed up downloading 50 web pages by 10x?

options.text: Whenever a thread executes an I/O operation (like waiting on network socket responses or disk reads), it releases the GIL, allowing other threads to run concurrently while the first thread waits.
ThreadPoolExecutor spawns real OS-level subprocesses under the hood instead of threads, so each download runs in its own process with its own independent GIL.
Downloading 50 pages is CPU-bound work (parsing HTML), and the GIL is released automatically for any function call that takes longer than 100 milliseconds, regardless of what it's doing.
The GIL is only enforced on the main thread; any thread created via threading.Thread or ThreadPoolExecutor is automatically exempt from GIL restrictions in CPython 3.9+.

explanation: Specification answer: Whenever a thread executes an I/O operation (like waiting on network socket responses or disk reads), it releases the GIL, allowing other threads to run concurrently while the first thread waits.

question: Race Conditions: What is a Race Condition, and what code construct is used to protect shared mutable state in multi-threaded programs?

options.text: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access and mutate shared data concurrently, causing non-deterministic data loss. It is resolved using threading.Lock (or threading.RLock) to create a mutually exclusive critical section.
A race condition occurs whenever two threads read the same variable at the same time; it's resolved with threading.Event, which pauses all but one thread until the value is read.
A race condition only happens across separate processes, never within threads of the same process, because threads already share the same memory and are inherently synchronized by the GIL.
A race condition is fixed by declaring the shared variable global inside every function that touches it; the global keyword itself provides the mutual exclusion needed for thread safety.

explanation: Specification answer: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access and mutate shared data concurrently, causing non-deterministic data loss. It is resolved using threading.Lock (or threading.RLock) to create a mutually exclusive critical section.

During triage in Concurrency Threading Multiprocessing, an engineer observes:
"Corrupted or truncated output files from daemon threads: Daemon threads are forcibly terminated when the main thread finishes, leaving buffers unflushed.".
What is the verified root cause?

options.text: When Python's main thread exits, all daemon=True threads are terminated instantly without running finally: blocks or flushing open file streams.

daemon=True threads run with a higher OS thread priority than the main thread, so they finish writing before the main thread can exit, but a race in the OS file cache still occasionally truncates the last write.

The output files were opened with 'w' mode instead of 'a' mode, so each daemon thread overwrites the previous thread's output instead of appending, which looks like truncation but isn't related to thread termination.

Python buffers all file writes in a single shared buffer across every thread; daemon threads only appear corrupted because their writes interleave with the main thread's own writes to the same buffer.

explanation:
Root Cause: When Python's main thread exits, all daemon=True threads are terminated instantly without running finally: blocks or flushing open file streams.

Fix Resolution:
Use standard non-daemon threads or coordinate shutdown with a threading.Event() and explicit thread.join():

What is the verified root cause?

options.text: sharedcounter += 1 is not atomic in Python. It disassembles into LOADGLOBAL, LOADCONST, BINARYOP, STOREGLOBAL. If a thread switch occurs between load and store, the update is lost.

shared_counter += 1 is atomic at the bytecode level, but the GIL is released every 100 bytecode instructions by default, and the counter update happens to fall exactly on that boundary in this workload.
The counter was declared with the global keyword inside each worker function, and global variables in CPython require an explicit threading.Lock just to be read, not only to be written.

Each thread holds its own private copy of shared_counter due to thread-local storage being enabled by default in CPython threads; the final printed value only reflects whichever thread happened to finish last.
